title: Antimicrobial Biomimetic Coatings for Dental Implants: A Systematic Review
html: Implant-associated infections remain a major challenge in dental implant therapy, frequently leading to implant failure, prolonged treatment, additional surgical interventions, and increased healthcare costs. Conventional antimicrobial strategies are limited by antimicrobial resistance, finite durability, and their inability to provide sustained antimicrobial activity while promoting optimal biological integration. Biomimetic coatings, designed to emulate natural biological compositions, structures, or functions, have emerged as promising surface modification strategies capable of enhancing osseointegration while conferring antimicrobial activity. To systematically evaluate and synthesize the available evidence regarding the antimicrobial effectiveness of biomimetic coatings applied to dental implant surfaces. A comprehensive literature search was conducted on 15 July 2025 using PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL). In vitro, in vivo, and clinical studies evaluating the antimicrobial performance of biomimetic coatings on dental implants were included. Study selection and data extraction followed PRISMA guidelines. Methodological quality and risk of bias were assessed using the Quality Assessment Tool for In Vitro Studies (QUIN) for in vitro investigations and the Systematic Review Centre for Laboratory Animal Experimentation (SYRCLE) Risk of Bias tool for animal studies. Twelve studies met the inclusion criteria, comprising predominantly in vitro investigations. The in vitro studies demonstrated moderate methodological quality, with recurrent limitations in sample size calculation, randomization, blinding, and reporting transparency. The animal studies exhibited a predominantly unclear risk of bias because of insufficient reporting across several methodological domains. Across the included studies, selected biomimetic coatings were associated with reductions in bacterial viability, metabolic activity, adhesion, surface colonization, or biofilm-related outcomes compared with control surfaces. However, these outcomes represented distinct biological endpoints, and the magnitude and consistency of the effects varied according to coating formulation, microorganism, experimental model, exposure period, and assessment method. Several studies also reported favorable cytocompatibility or osteogenic outcomes, although these findings were predominantly derived from short-term laboratory models. Biomimetic coatings show promising preclinical antimicrobial and osteogenic potential for dental implant applications. However, clinical effectiveness, long-term safety, coating stability, and resistance to mechanical wear and corrosion remain unestablished. The evidence is derived predominantly from heterogeneous in-vitro studies, supported by limited animal evidence and no clinical studies.
